Hook.voiceover: With one install command and a few lines of Python, you can find cars, buses and bottles in any photo or video. The code is short. The real decisions are the confidence threshold, and the licence. Let us make both decisions well.

Explain.voiceover: In the last lesson, you learned how to score boxes with IoU. Today, we produce those boxes with a real detector, on photos and on video.

slide.title: Running YOLO on Images and Video

Explain.voiceover: YOLO stands for you only look once. It is a family of fast object detectors that predict all boxes, classes and scores in one pass over the image, which makes them popular for video. We use the open-source Ultralytics Python package, which runs several YOLO versions with the same simple interface.

slide.title: You Only Look Once
slide.body: One image → one pass through the model → all boxes, classes and scores at once. Label: ultralytics Python package.

Explain.voiceover: The pre-trained models already know many common objects, such as cars, buses and bottles. They come in sizes, and the nano size is the smallest and fastest. Model names change with each new release, so check the current name before you start.

slide.title: Pre-trained models
slide.body: Know many common objects: car · bus · truck · bottle · Sizes: n (nano) = smallest, fastest · Names change with releases

Explain.voiceover: The key setting is the confidence threshold. Detections with a lower score are dropped. A low threshold keeps more real objects, but adds false alarms. A high threshold gives fewer false alarms, but misses small, distant or hidden objects. In other words, lowering it usually raises recall and lowers precision.

slide.title: The confidence threshold
slide.body: Low (0.1): more objects found, more false alarms, higher recall. High (0.7): fewer false alarms, misses small or distant objects, higher precision.

Explain.voiceover: It works like the sensitivity setting on a metal detector at the beach. Very sensitive, and it beeps for every coin and every bottle cap. Less sensitive, and it ignores the bottle caps, but also misses small coins buried deep.

And one more decision before you build anything real. Free to download does not mean free for any commercial use. You must check the Ultralytics YOLO licence before commercial use, and ask a legal adviser if you are unsure.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Lars Eriksson plans lorry traffic at a container port in Gothenburg, Sweden. He tests whether a pre-trained model detects trucks and cars in photos from a public road camera, with no people in close view.
Demonstrate.stock_query: lorries driving on road near container port

Demonstrate.voiceover: In a new Colab notebook, he installs the package and waits for it to finish. Then he uploads the road photo and runs the first cell. It loads the nano model, detects objects at a threshold of zero point two five, prints each one, and saves a copy with the boxes drawn.
screen_steps: In a new Colab notebook, run !pip install ultralytics and wait for it to finish
Run the first cell: YOLO('yolo11n.pt'), model('port_road.jpg', conf=0.25), print name, score and box, r.save

Demonstrate.voiceover: He opens the saved image. You'll see something like a truck with a score of zero point eight eight, inside a clear box. Each printed line shows the class name, the score, and the four corner values of the box in pixels, the same corner format as in the last lesson.
screen_steps: Open port_road_boxes.jpg from the file panel
Point to the printed line for the truck and its box

Demonstrate.voiceover: Now the thresholds. You'll see something like eleven detections at zero point one, six at zero point two five, and four at zero point five. At the lowest value, he finds two false alarms. A container stack is called a truck, and a road sign is called a stop sign. At the highest, one distant car is missed.
screen_steps: Run the loop over conf 0.1, 0.25 and 0.5
Display the 0.1 result and point out the two false alarms
Display the 0.5 result and point out the missed distant car

Demonstrate.voiceover: He chooses zero point two five for now, and notes that he must test it on more images. For video, he runs predict on the clip in streaming mode, which returns one result per frame and keeps memory low. With saving switched on, an annotated video appears in the output folder, and he plays it.
screen_steps: Run model.predict('port_road.mp4', conf=0.25, stream=True, save=True) in a loop
Open the saved video from runs/detect/ and play it

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to pick a threshold on one image and use it everywhere. A value that works on a clear daytime photo may miss most objects at night or in rain. Test on varied images.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, the Ultralytics package runs pre-trained YOLO models on images and video in a few lines, and returns boxes, classes and scores. Second, the confidence threshold trades false alarms against missed objects, so choose it by testing on varied images. Third, check the licence before any commercial use, because terms can change.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. ultralytics: boxes, classes, scores in a few lines. 2. Threshold = false alarms vs misses; test on varied images. 3. Check the licence before commercial use.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will run a pre-trained YOLO model on five images and one short video, try three thresholds, and record what changes. Choose scenes with objects and vehicles. It takes about thirty-five minutes. In the next lesson, Training YOLO on a Custom Dataset. See you there.
